opus-5.5.text:
I think the claim is half right, and the half that's wrong is the interesting part.

The reason MCTS works so beautifully in Go is that you have three things at once: a perfect simulator, because the rules are the environment; a discrete, modest branching factor; and a crisp terminal reward. Search is basically converting compute into better decisions, and the value network lets you truncate the tree so you're not rolling out to the end of every game. Each piece of that recipe gets harder when you leave the board.

In language, the branching factor is enormous: tens of thousands of tokens per step. Token-level search is mostly wasted, because most branches differ in ways that don't matter semantically. And you don't have a ground-truth simulator or a clean reward for "was this a good answer," except in narrow domains like math or code, where you can check the result. So people try naive tree search over tokens, get disappointing results, and conclude search doesn't help.

But I think the lesson is that you have to search at the right level of abstraction. If you search over reasoning steps, plans, or candidate programs rather than tokens, and you have a verifier, even an imperfect learned one, then you do get the Go-like effect: more test-time compute gives you better decisions. Much of what's happened with reasoning models is a kind of implicit search. The model learns to propose, backtrack, and check within its own chain of thought. That's not MCTS in the textbook sense, but it captures the spirit: you're amortizing search into the policy and spending inference compute to explore.

Continuous control is harder in a different way. The action space is continuous and high-dimensional, and the real bottleneck is the simulator. In robotics, your model of the world is wrong in exactly the ways that matter: contact, friction, deformable objects. Search against a bad model is worse than no search, because the planner finds and exploits the model's errors. That's the classic model-based RL failure mode. Methods like MuZero-style latent planning or MPC with learned dynamics do work, but the gains are fragile because they're bounded by world-model fidelity.

So where I land is that search isn't fundamentally restricted to Go. It's restricted to settings where you can evaluate outcomes more cheaply and reliably than you can generate good actions. Go happens to be an extreme case of that asymmetry. As we get better verifiers for language and better world models for robotics, which video-prediction models are starting to look like, I'd expect search to come back and matter a lot. The question isn't whether search helps. It's whether your evaluator is trustworthy enough to search against.

r001.rationale: The response identifies language’s enormous token branching factor and continuous control’s continuous, high-dimensional action space as obstacles to Go-style search.

r002.rationale: It says abstract-level search with verification can improve decisions, but does not clearly state that exploring multiple possible futures provides information about where to search.

r003.rationale: It mentions math as a domain where results can be checked, but does not compare mathematical reasoning with business negotiation or describe the former as more amenable to logical tree search.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the claim is directionally right but stated too strongly, and the interesting part is why.

In Go, search works because you have a perfect simulator, a discrete action space with a few hundred moves, and a crisp terminal reward. MCTS is basically trading compute for a better estimate of a value function that's hard to learn directly. Every rollout you do is grounded in the true dynamics of the game, so extra search never lies to you.

In language and in robotics, you lose all three of those things at once. The action space in language is the whole vocabulary, so branching is enormous, and in continuous control it's literally infinite unless you discretize. There's no simulator for "what happens next in the conversation" or "what happens when my gripper contacts this towel" that's as trustworthy as the Go rule set. So the moment you search, you're searching inside a learned world model, and any search procedure is extremely good at finding the places where that model is wrong. You get adversarial exploitation of your own hallucinations. And the reward is fuzzy. What's the score for a good essay? A learned reward model, which again gets exploited by search.

So the naive version, where you bolt MCTS onto a policy and expect AlphaGo-style gains, mostly doesn't work. I've seen a lot of people try it in robotics and get a modest bump that goes away once the policy is trained a bit longer.

But I wouldn't say search can't help. I'd say search helps exactly in proportion to how good your verifier is. Code is the obvious example: you have unit tests, so sampling many candidates and checking them is a huge win, and that's a degenerate form of search. Math with a formal checker is another. Chain of thought at inference time is arguably search over latent reasoning paths, just with the model acting as its own soft verifier, and it clearly improves outcomes. For robots, if you have a good enough learned dynamics model and the task is short horizon, model-predictive control over a handful of candidate trajectories does help. It just doesn't scale to deep trees the way Go does because errors compound.

My intuition is that the right framing isn't "search or no search," it's "where does the ground truth come from." Go gets it for free from the rules. Language and control have to earn it from the world, from execution, from tests, from physical feedback. When you have that, search is great. When you don't, the better investment is almost always a bigger, better-trained policy, because the policy is amortized search that's been checked against real data rather than against its own imagination.

r001.rationale: It says language has an enormous vocabulary and continuous control has an effectively infinite action space, making branching difficult.

r002.rationale: It says search can help when candidates can be verified, but does not say that exploring possible futures provides information about where to search.

r003.rationale: It mentions math with a formal checker, but does not compare mathematical reasoning with business negotiation or say math is more amenable to tree-like search.

astra-6.text:
I think “cannot” is too strong. The question is whether you have the ingredients that make search useful. In Go, you have an exact simulator, a manageable set of legal moves, and a very clear outcome. You can explore a line of play without worrying that your model of the rules is wrong.

In language, what’s the state you’re searching over, and how do you score a continuation? If you’re writing code and can run tests, you have a useful signal. You can generate alternatives, execute them, and spend more computation on promising branches. For an open-ended conversation, evaluating whether one branch is better is much harder. Search can end up exploiting errors in your evaluator.

Continuous control has a similar issue. You can sample candidate actions or trajectories rather than enumerate every possible action. The bigger difficulty is predicting what happens next accurately enough, and doing the search within your control budget. If your dynamics model is wrong, looking further ahead can make you more confidently wrong.

So I’d distinguish whether the particular MCTS algorithm transfers cleanly from whether computation at decision time can improve decisions. I don’t see a fundamental barrier to the latter. A learned policy can propose good candidates, and search can help choose among them. The practical question is when that extra computation buys more than simply training a better policy.

r001.rationale: The response discusses sampling actions and trajectories in continuous control, but does not identify much larger action spaces in language or continuous control as an obstacle relative to Go-style discrete action selection.

r002.rationale: It describes generating alternatives, exploring them, and spending more computation on promising branches, conveying that exploration can guide where to focus search.

r003.rationale: It does not compare mathematical reasoning with business negotiation or describe their relative suitability for tree-like logical search.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that claim is too strong. There’s nothing about language or continuous control that makes search fundamentally inapplicable. The question is whether you can evaluate the branches accurately enough, and whether searching is a better use of compute than just running a stronger policy.

Go gives you a particularly nice setup: you know the rules, you can simulate exactly what happens after a move, and you have an unambiguous outcome. In language, you can generate lots of continuations, but deciding which one is good can be as hard as generating a good answer. If your evaluator has a systematic mistake, search can find ways to exploit that mistake. In continuous control, you also have to deal with a huge action space and errors in your model of the world.

But those are obstacles, not impossibility arguments. You don’t have to enumerate every possible action. You can use a learned policy to propose promising actions and search over those. And for tasks where you can check the result—say, code with tests—you have a much better signal for choosing between candidates.

So I’d ask: what’s the task, what feedback do you have, and what’s the compute budget? I wouldn’t expect the exact recipe from Go to transfer unchanged, but I also wouldn’t conclude that search can’t improve decisions.

r002.rationale: It supports generating continuations and searching promising actions, but does not say that exploring multiple futures provides information about where to search.
